planting.note: Sow seed in fall onto the surface of moist, acidic, low-nutrient sandy or peaty soil so winter cold can break dormancy, mimicking the bogs, seepage slopes, and wet pine savannas where it grows wild.

directions: Sow seed in fall onto the surface of moist, acidic, low-nutrient sandy or peaty soil so winter cold can break dormancy, mimicking the bogs, seepage slopes, and wet pine savannas where it grows wild. The flame-orange, densely packed flower spikes are unmistakable and bloom over a long season from late spring through fall, drawing bumblebees, small native bees, and butterflies looking for nectar in low-fertility wetland habitats. It performs poorly in rich or fertilized garden soil and is best suited to a dedicated bog garden, rain garden, or restored savanna planting kept consistently damp. Established plants may act as short-lived perennials, reseeding themselves modestly if conditions stay favorably wet and open.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container transplants in spring into lean, dry, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil — it is native to limestone glades and dry prairies of the Gulf South and Ozark region and resents wet feet or rich soil.

directions: Plant divisions or container transplants in spring into lean, dry, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil — it is native to limestone glades and dry prairies of the Gulf South and Ozark region and resents wet feet or rich soil. The evergreen grass-like basal foliage forms a tidy, low groundcover topped in late spring and early summer by clusters of small, rayless golden-yellow flower heads that are surprisingly showy en masse and highly attractive to small native bees and butterflies. Because it lacks the aggressive rhizomes of many goldenrods, it stays a well-behaved clump rather than spreading into surrounding beds. It is an excellent, increasingly popular substitute for turf or mulch in hot, dry, sunny native plantings.

planting.note: Scarify seed coat and soak 24 hours, then direct sow in fall into deep, dry, infertile sand in full sun; this taprooted lupine of longleaf pine sandhills does not transplant well once established and needs excellent drainage year-round.

directions: Scarify and direct sow in fall into deep, dry, infertile sand in full sun, since this taprooted lupine of longleaf pine sandhills does not transplant well once established and needs excellent drainage year-round. Silvery, hairy foliage emerges in winter followed by dense spikes of sky-blue, pea-like flowers in early spring, making it one of the showiest and earliest native wildflowers of the Gulf Coast sandhills. It is an essential larval host plant for the increasingly rare frosted elfin butterfly, so preserving or planting it directly supports a species of real conservation concern. Never fertilize or irrigate beyond establishment, since rich or moist conditions quickly kill this drought-adapted native.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall directly into consistently wet to seasonally flooded, acidic, sandy soil along pond edges, ditches, and pine savanna wetlands, since it germinates poorly without a season of natural cold-moist stratification.

directions: Sow seed in fall directly into consistently wet to seasonally flooded, acidic, sandy soil along pond edges, ditches, and pine savanna wetlands, since it germinates poorly without a season of natural cold-moist stratification. Slender, nearly leafless hollow stems rise from a cluster of thin basal leaflets and open into flat white umbels of tiny flowers in late summer, resembling a delicate wild carrot relative built for standing water. As a member of the carrot family it is an important larval host plant for black swallowtail butterflies in wetland habitats, and its late flowers also draw small native bees, wasps, and flies. Keep the root zone wet through the growing season; it is not suited to average garden beds that dry out between waterings.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall onto the surface of moist, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded woodland edge or savanna margin, since seed needs a full season of cold exposure and light to break dormancy, or plant nursery-grown transplants in fall to skip the slow seedling stage.

directions: Sow fresh seed in fall onto the surface of moist, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded woodland edge or savanna margin, since seed needs a full season of cold exposure and light to break dormancy, or plant nursery-grown transplants in fall to skip the slow seedling stage. This tall, downy-stemmed relative of the carrot family produces broad umbels of small greenish-white flowers in late summer, providing a late-season nectar source for wasps, flies, beetles, and native bees when few other woodland plants are blooming. It also serves as a larval host plant for black swallowtail butterflies, extending that species' host range into shadier habitats than the sun-loving carrot family usually occupies. Despite the species name it is not seriously dangerous to handle; the name references its resemblance to more toxic relatives, so simply avoid ingestion as with any wild member of this plant family.
